155.title: When you miss a day
155.hook: in a 2009 study, missing one day didn't derail a forming habit (Lally et al.)
155.tomorrow: Camp 3 close: the practice is yours
155.howItsDone: Habit researchers and coaches usually advise treating a missed day as a small gap rather than a failure, and simply resuming the next day without trying to make up for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one-breath version of everything, for the hard days. Your line was one breath counts. What did your smallest versions turn out to be? Day one hundred fifty-five.

It will happen. Maybe not this week, maybe not this month, but one day you'll miss. Not even the one-breath version. You'll get to bedtime and realize the whole day went by without a single practice. And then comes the dangerous part, which isn't the missed day at all. It's the voice afterward. Well, that's ruined. I always do this. I'm just not a person who sticks with things. That voice can end a good habit faster than any busy day. So let's meet it now, while things are calm. Today's practice is when you miss a day.
screen: `A WHOLE DAY, NOTHING.` → `WELL, THAT'S RUINED.` → `WHEN YOU MISS A DAY.`

segments.voice: In 2009, a team at University College London led by Phillippa Lally followed ninety-six volunteers for twelve weeks. Each picked one new daily habit, like a glass of water with lunch or a short run before dinner, and reported every day how automatic it felt. Two findings stand out. First, it took much longer than the twenty-one days you sometimes hear. The typical time to reach something like automatic was about sixty-six days, and for some people far longer. So if you still have to remember your practices on purpose, you're not failing. You're on schedule. Second, and this is the one to keep: missing a single day did not meaningfully set people back. The habit curve kept climbing. One gap didn't break the chain. What does break it is the story we tell about the gap. If one missed day becomes proof you're hopeless, you stop. If it's just a missed day, you start again tomorrow. You already know how to do this. Back on day one hundred, counting breaths, the instruction was: when you lose count, start again at one. No scolding. No starting over from scratch as a person. Just one. And Seneca, reviewing his day, ended with: see that you don't do it again; this time I forgive you. So the practice is to restart without a speech. No apology, no big plan to make up for it, no doubling up tomorrow to compensate. Just do today's practice, today. The missed day is already behind you. The next breath isn't.
screen: `NINETY-SIX VOLUNTEERS, 2009.` · `ABOUT SIXTY-SIX DAYS.` · `ONE MISS DIDN'T BREAK IT.` · `START AGAIN AT ONE.` · then, large: `JUST START AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the restart. Settle, and breathe. Imagine it's the morning after a missed day. Notice the voice getting ready to give its speech. Let it start, and then gently cut it off. No speech. Just begin: one breath, the first of your five. Feel how light that is. Then keep breathing, starting again at one whenever your mind wanders. The bell holds the time.
Habit curve, the gradual rise researchers found toward a habit feeling automatic, which one missed day doesn't meaningfully set back. Today's word.
Your line: just start again. Write it at the bottom of your list of five, so it's there the morning you need it. Day one hundred fifty-five.

screen: `DAY 155 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CAMP 3 CLOSE: THE PRACTICE IS YOURS.`

156.title: Camp 3 close: the practice is yours
156.hook: sixty days of tools; next, a poet and an emperor
156.howItsDone: People who keep a personal spiritual practice outside a single tradition often settle on a short daily routine of a few practices, such as breath, a morning intention, an evening review and a walk, and adjust it over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the habit curve, the missed day, and the restart without a speech. Your line was just start again. Is it written at the bottom of your list? Day one hundred fifty-six.

Sixty days ago, this camp started with a promise in four words: I can do this. Not I understand this, or I've read about this. Do. Back then, practice might have sounded like something other people did: monks, athletes, people with more time. Look at what you've done since. You've watched ten breaths and sighed on purpose. You've previewed mornings and reviewed evenings. You've sorted worries into mine and not mine, counted good things, looked down from a mile up, and remembered you will die. You've walked, scanned, slept, served, hidden your phone and watched the sun go. Today, the last day of the camp, we put it together. Today is camp three close.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS AGO: I CAN DO THIS.` → `LOOK WHAT YOU'VE DONE.` → `CAMP THREE CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole camp, in order. Week one: breath, from just watching to box breathing. Week two: bookends, Marcus's morning preview and Seneca's evening review. Week three: the dichotomy of control, Epictetus's two columns. Week four: gratitude, three good things and grace before meals. Week five: the view from above, the pale blue dot, memento mori and the Buddha's five remembrances. Week six: walking, kayagatasati and sleep. Week seven: service, one act a week. Week eight: the digital sabbath, borrowed with respect from Shabbat. Week nine: sunset as a ritual. And this last week: your five, their smallest versions, and starting again. The Stoics had a word for all this: askesis, training, the way an athlete trains. Epictetus taught that philosophy isn't only for reading; it's exercise, done daily, in small reps. Dictionaries trace the English word ascetic to the same Greek root, but the older sense is simpler: practice. And that's what this camp was. Not beliefs to adopt. Nobody on this path has told you what to believe. Tools, borrowed carefully from traditions and from science, each named, each left in its own home. What you do with them is yours. Now the path turns. The next camp is about a text, read slowly: two books, side by side. One by a thirteenth-century Persian poet, a Muslim scholar named Jalal al-Din Rumi. One by a second-century Roman emperor, writing private notes to himself: Marcus Aurelius, whom you've already met. Two voices, never merged.
screen: `NINE WEEKS OF TOOLS.` · `ASKESIS: TRAINING.` · `TOOLS, NOT BELIEFS.` · `NEXT: A POET AND AN EMPEROR.` · then, large: `I CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your whole routine once, in its smallest form. Settle. For your first practice, one breath's worth. Then the second. Then the third, the fourth, the fifth. If one is a walk or a sunset, picture it for a breath. When you've done all five, rest, and feel it: that was your whole routine, and it fit inside two minutes. Say inside: I can do this. The bell holds the time.
Askesis, the Greek word for training, the exercise-like daily practice the Stoics believed philosophy required. Today's word.
Your line: I can do this. Today, do your whole routine once, at full size if you can, smallest size if you can't. Both count. Tomorrow, two books. Day one hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 156 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO BOOKS FOR ONE CAMP.`

157.title: Two books for one camp
157.hook: a Persian poet and a Roman emperor, read side by side, each in his own world
157.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often read a short entry each morning, and readers of Rumi's Masnavi traditionally read it slowly, story by story, sometimes in study circles, especially in Turkey, Iran and South Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, askesis, the whole practice camp, came together in one routine. Your line was I can do this. Did you do your five? Day one hundred fifty-seven, and a new camp.

Imagine two men who could never have met. One is a Roman emperor in a cold army camp by the Danube river, around the year 170, writing at night by lamplight in a private notebook, reminding himself how to be a decent person. The other is a Muslim scholar in the city of Konya, in what is now Turkey, a thousand years later, reciting long poems full of stories while a student writes them down. One speaks Greek, one Persian. One leans on reason, the other on longing for God. For the next seventy-five days, we'll read them side by side. Today's lesson is two books for one camp.
screen: `AN EMPEROR BY THE DANUBE.` → `A POET IN KONYA.` → `TWO BOOKS FOR ONE CAMP.`

segments.voice: The first book is the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. We've already met him: the view from above, the morning preview. He wrote it in Greek, not Latin, in twelve short books, and most scholars think he never meant anyone else to read it. The oldest manuscripts give it a title that means simply to himself. The name Meditations was added much later. So when you read it, you're reading someone's private notes: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself," one famous entry starts, and then lists the difficult people he expects to meet. The second book is the Masnavi of Jalal al-Din Rumi. It's enormous, about twenty-five thousand couplets in six books, in Persian, full of stories: merchants, parrots, kings, lovers, a reed flute. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and a teacher of Islamic law, steeped in the Qur'an, and the Masnavi is soaked in it. Some Persian speakers have called it the Qur'an in Persian, a phrase that tells you how deeply it's loved. Here is how this camp works. We read in paraphrase and in careful older translations, one story or one passage at a time. We keep each man in his own world. Marcus is a Stoic who trusts reason and duty. Rumi is a Muslim mystic who speaks of longing for God. We won't pretend they're saying the same thing, and we won't make one of them the winner. We'll just listen to each, and notice what happens in you when two different voices sit side by side.
screen: `TO HIMSELF: THE MEDITATIONS.` · `THE MASNAVI: SIX BOOKS OF STORIES.` · `EACH IN HIS OWN WORLD.` · `LISTEN TO EACH, NO WINNER.` · then, large: `TWO VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two different books. If you can, pick up two real books, any two, one in each hand. If not, rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and imagine them. Feel the weight of each: different sizes, different worlds. Don't choose between them. Just hold both, and let your breath move between your hands. The bell holds the time.
Masnavi, Rumi's long Persian poem of about twenty-five thousand couplets, read side by side with Marcus's notebook this camp. Today's word.
Your line: two voices. Today, when you hear two people disagree, try listening to each fully before deciding anything. Tomorrow, a boy leaves the east. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

158.title: A boy leaves the east
158.hook: Jalal al-Din is born around 1207 in the eastern Persian world, and his family walks west as the Mongols approach
158.howItsDone: Visitors from many countries travel to Konya, in Turkey, to the museum and tomb of Rumi, and his birthplace is honored in Afghanistan and Tajikistan as well; readers often start with the story of his family's long journey west.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Masnavi and Marcus's notebook, a Persian poet and a Roman emperor, side by side. Your line was two voices. Which one are you more curious about? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

Packing up a whole life looks much the same in any century. Boxes, a cart or a truck, the house you grew up in shrinking behind you. Now go back to around the year 1216, in the far east of the Persian-speaking world, near what is now northern Afghanistan. A respected preacher gathers his family, his books and his students, and starts walking west. His little son is about nine. The boy's name is Jalal al-Din Muhammad. He will not come back. Years later, when he's famous, people will call him by the name of the place where he ended up. Today, the boy who left the east.
screen: `PACKING UP A WHOLE LIFE.` → `AROUND 1216, WALKING WEST.` → `A BOY LEAVES THE EAST.`

segments.voice: Start with the birth. Tradition says Jalal al-Din was born in 1207 in Balkh, an old city of scholars. Some modern historians think it was really Vakhsh, a smaller town in today's Tajikistan, where his father was working at the time. Either way, he was born in the eastern Persian world, and Persian was his language. His father, Baha al-Din Walad, was a preacher and a teacher of religion, a serious man who wrote down his own inner life in a notebook the family kept. Then the leaving. Somewhere between 1216 and 1220 the family set out. The old accounts say they went ahead of the Mongols, whose armies swept through the region and wrecked Balkh around 1220. Some scholars add that Baha al-Din had quarrels at home too. We don't know every reason, and the sources don't agree. What we know is the road: Baghdad, a pilgrimage to Mecca, then years in towns across Anatolia, the land that is now Turkey. On the way the boy grew up, married young, and lost his mother. Around 1228 the family settled in Konya. And here's the thing to tell a friend tonight. Anatolia had once been part of the Roman Empire, so people in the east called it Rum, Rome. A man from Rum was Rumi. The name English readers know him by comes from where he landed, not where he started. Keep that road in mind all camp. Being far from where you began will come back again and again in what we read.
screen: `BORN 1207, EASTERN PERSIAN WORLD.` · `THE FAMILY WALKS WEST.` · `BAGHDAD, MECCA, ANATOLIA, KONYA.` · `RUMI MEANS FROM RUM, ROME.` · then, large: `THE ROAD WEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a place you left. A town, a house, a school, a country, a friendship. Settle and let it come. What did it smell like? What did the light do in the afternoon? Who was there? Don't judge whether leaving was right. Just let yourself stand there again for a minute. Then notice who you became because you left. The bell holds the time.
Balkh, the old city of scholars in today's Afghanistan where tradition says young Jalal al-Din was born. Today's word.
Your line: the road west. Today, when you pass something that reminds you of a place you left, say your line and notice what you carried with you. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: The scholar of Konya
159.hook: he becomes a respected teacher of Islamic law and theology in Konya, Anatolia
159.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi often begin with his life as a scholar: he taught Islamic law and theology in Konya, and biographies stress that his later poetry grew out of that learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy left Balkh and walked all the way to Konya. Your line was the road west. What did you carry from the place you left? Day one hundred fifty-nine.

Some people grow up into their parent's job. The kid who took over the family store, the doctor whose mother was a doctor, the pastor's son who became the pastor. People nod at them in the street. They're solid. They're safe. Konya, the early 1240s. A man in his mid-thirties, in a scholar's robe and a large turban, walks to teach his classes with students trailing behind him. People ask him legal questions and wait for his answer. He is exactly what everyone expected. If his life had stopped here, he might be remembered only as a learned man of Konya. Today, the scholar of Konya.
screen: `BECOMING YOUR PARENT'S JOB.` → `A ROBE, A TURBAN, STUDENTS.` → `THE SCHOLAR OF KONYA.`

segments.voice: Konya in the 1200s was the capital of the Seljuk sultans of Rum, a Muslim kingdom in Anatolia, full of mosques, schools and caravans. The sources say the sultan invited Rumi's father to teach there. Then, in 1231, the father died, and his post passed to his son, who was about twenty-four. That's young to inherit a pulpit. So the son kept studying. A former student of his father, Burhan al-Din of Tirmidh, came to Konya and, the accounts say, trained him for about nine years, in books and in the inner life of prayer and fasting. The young man also went to study in Aleppo and Damascus, two old centers of learning. By the early 1240s he was a respected teacher of Islamic law and theology, what Muslims call fiqh and kalam. He taught in a school, preached in the mosque, gave legal opinions, and was addressed as Mowlana, our master. He had a wife and sons. The oldest son, Sultan Walad, would one day write his father's story. Here's what's worth noticing. The sources show no sign yet of the poet. The sources describe a learned, careful, deeply religious man. The wildness came later, and it grew out of this ground, not against it. His poems are full of the Qur'an and of law and theology, because he'd spent his whole life inside them. Hold on to that. The respectable one was not a mask he later threw off. It was the soil.
screen: `KONYA, CAPITAL OF THE SELJUKS.` · `HIS FATHER'S POST AT TWENTY-FOUR.` · `NINE YEARS WITH BURHAN AL-DIN.` · `A TEACHER OF LAW AND THEOLOGY.` · then, large: `THE RESPECTABLE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you're known for. Settle, and breathe. If people who know you were asked to describe you in three words, what would they say? Reliable. Funny. The one who fixes things. The one who's always busy. Say the words inside. Then ask, gently: is that all of me? Is there something in me nobody has met yet? Don't answer quickly. Just leave the question open. The bell holds the time.
Mowlana, our master: the title Rumi's students used for him as a teacher of Islamic law and theology. Today's word.
Your line: the respectable one. Today, when someone treats you as the dependable version of yourself, say your line, and let it be true without being the whole story. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

160.title: Shams arrives
160.hook: in 1244 a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, meets Rumi, and his life turns (the accounts are part history, part legend)
160.howItsDone: The meeting of Rumi and Shams is told in the old biographies by Sipahsalar and Aflaki, which blend history and legend, and readers of Rumi still retell it as the turning point of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mowlana, robe, turban, students, his father's post. Your line was the respectable one. Did anyone meet the other parts of you? Day one hundred sixty.

Some people walk into your life and nothing is the same afterward. A teacher who saw something in you. A stranger on a train. The person you married. You can usually name the day. For Rumi, the day was in the autumn of 1244. He was about thirty-seven, settled, respected, sure of his path. Into Konya came an older man, perhaps in his sixties, a wandering dervish in a rough cloak, from the city of Tabriz. He had no school, no post and no patience for either. His name was Shams, which means sun. Today, Shams arrives.
screen: `YOU CAN NAME THE DAY.` → `KONYA, AUTUMN 1244.` → `SHAMS ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: First the honest part. Much of what we're told about this meeting comes from biographies written decades later by devoted followers, and they read partly as history and partly as legend. So hold the stories lightly. One story goes like this. Rumi is riding through the market with his students. Shams grabs his bridle and asks him a question. Who was greater, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or the Sufi Bayazid, who said startling things about his own closeness to God? Rumi answers: the Prophet. Bayazid's thirst was quenched by one sip; the Prophet's thirst was endless, and he kept asking for more. In some tellings Rumi faints. In another story, Shams throws the scholar's books into water, then pulls them out dry. Nobody can prove any of it. What is solid is what happened next. The two men shut themselves away for weeks, maybe months, talking, praying, fasting. Rumi stopped teaching. His students were furious and jealous. Who was this beggar who had taken their master? We even have Shams's own voice, because his sayings were written down in a book called the Maqalat, the Discourses. He comes across as blunt, funny and fierce, impatient with people who knew about God from books but had never tasted anything. The respected scholar had met someone who asked him whether he knew what he knew. And he answered by changing his life.
screen: `PART HISTORY, PART LEGEND.` · `A QUESTION IN THE MARKET.` · `WEEKS AWAY; STUDENTS FURIOUS.` · `SHAMS'S OWN VOICE: THE MAQALAT.` · then, large: `SOMEONE ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall a meeting that changed you. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind whose arrival turned something. It might have been gentle or rough, long ago or last year. Where were you? What did they say, or what did they just do? What changed afterward? If you can, feel a little gratitude, even if it was hard. If they're still alive, notice whether they know what they did. The bell holds the time.
Shams arrives. In 1244 a wandering dervish from Tabriz meets the scholar of Konya, and Rumi's life turns. Today's word.
Your line: someone arrives. Today, treat one ordinary encounter as if it might matter: look up, listen fully, and ask one real question. Day one hundred sixty.

161.title: Shams disappears
161.hook: Shams leaves, returns, and vanishes for good around 1247, and Rumi's grief becomes poetry
161.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi usually meet this grief through the Divan of Shams of Tabriz, his collection of lyric poems, many of which close with Shams's name where a poet would sign his own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger from Tabriz grabbed a scholar's bridle in the market. Your line was someone arrives. Who did you really listen to? Day one hundred sixty-one.

You've probably seen someone grieve out loud. Not quietly, not politely. The friend who played the same song forty times after the breakup. The widower who talked about his wife to everyone at the grocery store. Grief that has to go somewhere. Rumi's life had just been turned upside down by a friend. Then the friend left. Then he came back. Then, one winter night around 1247, he was gone, and nobody ever saw him again. The respectable scholar did something no one in Konya expected. He began to sing. Today, Shams disappears.

segments.voice: Here's the story as the sources give it. Rumi's students resented Shams for taking their teacher away. After about sixteen months, in early 1246, Shams slipped out of Konya and went to Damascus. Rumi was desolate. He sent his son Sultan Walad all the way to Syria to bring him back, and Shams came. For a while things were good. Then the resentment returned, and around December 1247 Shams vanished for good. What happened? Honestly, nobody knows. A later story says he was murdered, and even names one of Rumi's own sons as involved. Historians such as Franklin Lewis doubt that story, and there's no proof. Other accounts say he simply left, as he'd left places all his life. Rumi went looking. He traveled to Damascus, searching the streets. And somewhere in the search, the tradition says, he stopped looking outside. He began to feel that what he loved in Shams was already speaking through him. And he wrote. Out of this loss came a huge collection of lyric poems, thousands of them; tradition says many were composed aloud, some while he turned to music. It's called the Divan of Shams of Tabriz, because at the end of many poems, where a poet usually signs his own name, Rumi signed his friend's. He gave his poems away to the one he'd lost. Grief didn't go quiet in him. It became music. That's what your line means: the grief sang.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line for someone gone. Let one person come to mind: someone who died, moved away, or drifted off. Settle, and breathe with them near. Then find one line. It doesn't have to be poetry. It can be a thing they used to say, or what you'd tell them now, or just their name and a color. Say it inside, or write it down. Let the missing be there without fixing it. The bell holds the time.
Shams disappears. Around 1247 Rumi's friend vanished for good, and Rumi's grief poured out as thousands of poems signed with Shams's name. Today's word.
